Project report

OcuVal

A study of whether software that finds fluid in eye scans still works on a scanner brand it was never trained on, built and documented the way medical device software is.

Not for clinical use. This is a research and portfolio project built on public challenge data. It has never been used on patients, has not been validated for patient care, and makes no clinical claim of any kind.

At a glance

70OCT scans, one per patient
3scanner brands
3training runs, each leaving one brand out
6sealed test sets, each evaluated once under the final seeded procedure
about 0.14smallest Dice difference this design can detect
0non-deterministic GPU fallbacks recorded, across 9 determinism records (what this does and does not show)

The question: if a model learns from two scanner brands, does it work as well on a third it has never seen? The answer: no difference could be established, in any of 9 pre-registered comparisons. The study can only detect gaps larger than about 0.14 Dice, so this does not show that the model works on the new brand.

In plain words

An OCT scan uses light to take cross-section pictures of the back of the eye, a bit like an ultrasound but far finer. In some common eye diseases, fluid collects in or under the retina, and doctors watch how much there is to decide on treatment and to see whether it is working. I trained a model that outlines three kinds of this fluid in OCT scans: fluid within the retina (IRF), fluid under it (SRF), and pockets where its bottom layer lifts away (PED).

Hospitals use scanners from different companies whose images look different, so I asked: if the model learns from two brands, does it still work on a third it has never seen? The honest answer is that I could not detect a difference, but this test could only have detected a large one. The aim was a trustworthy measurement rather than the highest score, and part of why the scores are modest is a pattern described under Findings: the model marks fluid in scans that have none of that type.

Dataset

The data is the training partition of the RETOUCH challenge: 70 scans, one per patient, each with expert outlines of the three fluid types. I did not take the challenge's official test partition, so every result here comes from these 70 scans (docs/06 §2.1). The scan geometry and the share of voxels that are fluid were measured from the archive (docs/06 §3.1, §3.1.2, §3.2). The counts of scans containing each fluid type come from the evaluation records.

Fluid occupies a tiny share of each scan, which is why accuracy is never reported here: a model that marks nothing would score very high on it.

Study design

I trained the model 3 times. Each run holds one brand out entirely and trains on the other two. Its score on the unseen brand is compared with its score on new patients from the brands it learned from, the familiar-brand test set. Every patient falls in exactly one box of each diagram, and a test that gates every change to the code checks that no patient appears in two (TC-004). Both test sets were sealed: the code refuses to read them without a recorded reason and approval, and logs every access.

How results are measured

Dice
Overlap between the model's outline and the expert's, from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (perfect). A scan without a fluid type scores 1 if the model marks none of it, and 0 if it marks any.
HD95
How far, in millimetres, one outline's boundary strays from the other's: the distance that 95% of boundary points stay within, taking the worse of the two directions.
Sensitivity
Of the scans that contain a fluid type, the share the model calls present. A type counts as present when the model marks more than 10 voxels of it.
Specificity
Of the scans without a fluid type, the share the model calls absent, at the same threshold.
AUROC
How well the model's confidence ranks scans with a fluid type above scans without it, across every possible threshold at once. It needs no threshold, which makes it the fairer view here.
Patient-level bootstrap interval
A 95% interval made by resampling patients, not scans or pixels, 2000 times with a fixed seed, so it reflects how much the result would move with different patients.
Pre-registration
The analysis was written down and committed before any result was seen. Anything decided afterwards is labelled post-hoc wherever it appears.

Each run's model was scored on the unseen brand and on the familiar-brand test set. Every figure carries its 95% interval and the number of patients it rests on. The model output is the average of 20 passes with dropout switched on, seeded per scan so that it can be reproduced exactly.

* AUROC has no interval. The per-scan confidence score was not saved in the sealed records, so an interval cannot be computed without opening them again (docs/08 D9). Under each AUROC are its scans with and without the fluid type, and under each HD95 the patients it rests on: HD95 is undefined when exactly one of the two outlines is empty, so its n can be smaller. An interval over one patient has no spread and is marked as such.

What this design can and cannot detect

Half the width of a difference interval is the smallest observed difference that would exclude zero. Here that is 0.14 to 0.29 Dice for a single run and 0.14 to 0.18 with the runs pooled. A true difference of exactly that size would be detected only about half the time. So this design cannot detect a difference between brands smaller than about 0.14 Dice, and detects differences within a single run below about 0.3 unreliably. The limit comes from the familiar-brand test sets, which hold 7 patients per run. This analysis is post-hoc (docs/10 §5.4).

Findings

The model marks fluid in scans that have none of that type

In 14 of 18 groups (run, test set and fluid type), every scan without that fluid type got the worst possible score: the model marked a little of it anyway. The score treats that as a complete miss, which drags the average down. For SRF and PED, the familiar-brand test sets happened to contain more such scans (62% against 47% for SRF and 77% against 53% for PED, pooled), so part of those comparisons reflects which scans were in each group rather than the scanner brand. The split into present and absent scans was planned before the Spectralis and Topcon results and is post-hoc for Cirrus; the case-mix comparison is post-hoc (docs/10 §5.2, §7.1).

Detection: almost every fluid type is called present in almost every scan

Sensitivity is perfect in all 18 groups and specificity is zero in 13 of 18: at the fixed threshold the model calls almost every fluid type present in almost every scan. Its confidence still ranks scans well, with AUROC from 0.95 to 1.00 on every unseen brand. The fixed operating point is the weak part, not the ranking.

With few patients, the score is fragile

If one scan without a fluid type flips between "nothing marked" and "a few voxels marked", its Dice jumps from 1 to 0, and a 7-patient average moves by 0.1429. I saw a shift of about that size between two equally valid evaluations of the same model, before I made evaluation reproducible: Cirrus familiar-brand SRF moved from 0.2707 to 0.1276, a change of 0.1431, in a group with 4 SRF-free scans. The older run did not keep per-scan scores, so I cannot confirm that a single scan caused it (docs/10 §7.2).

What the outlines look like

These B-scans were chosen by a rule I committed before rendering any image (docs/07 §21), from the numbers in the sealed records alone: the worst, median and best unseen-brand scans by Dice, and the largest false-positive case for each fluid type. Each shows the prediction that was evaluated, regenerated and checked to match its sealed record exactly before it was saved. They are illustrations, not results, and they are not typical. The challenge organiser gave written permission for a very small number of illustrative images (docs/06 §2.2.2); no case identifier, brand or date appears in them.

Training

Reproducibility

  • Training repeats exactly. Two short training runs of the same configuration on this GPU produced byte-identical weights, optimiser state and epoch logs (TC-121). Two differently configured runs agree on every recorded value through epoch 5, and first differ at epoch 6, where their learning-rate schedules diverge (TC-123).
  • No recorded fallbacks. The 9 determinism records of the final training runs and sealed evaluations show 0 fallbacks to non-repeatable GPU methods. That means no operation announced itself as non-repeatable; it does not by itself prove two runs agree, which is why runs were also compared directly.
  • Evaluation repeats exactly. Before any sealed test set was opened, two seeded evaluations of the validation set had to match value for value. They matched on 466 of 466 values and all 21 per-scan rows.
  • Scope. These claims are proven on this workstation's GPU and software versions only.

Engineering and documentation

  • DICOM. All 70 scans are converted to standard medical imaging files and de-identified, with the result verified. Code for DICOM Segmentation and Structured Report outputs is built and tested; the round trip through a hospital-style image archive (PACS) is written but has never run, because Docker is not installed here. docs/11
  • IEC 62304 and ISO 14971. The software is documented following IEC 62304 as safety class B, with a risk file following ISO 14971 that identifies 16 hazards and 32 risk controls. docs/03, docs/05
  • Traceability. All 93 software requirements trace to a test case. Of 120 registered test cases, 96 are written and 93 are executed; 3 have never run because they need the PACS. A test in CI recomputes these counts and fails if the document disagrees. docs/09

Worth a closer look

A cross-check that caught a real defect before any result existed
I first computed HD95 by pooling both directions of boundary distance into one list. Every test passed, because every test was written from the same understanding as the code. A check against an independent library (MONAI, TC-120) disagreed on 5 of 12 random cases, and I adopted the standard definition before reporting anything. docs/13
Refusing to make up scan details the data does not contain
The dataset does not record which eye was scanned, but the DICOM standard requires that field. The code refuses to invent a value, or under an explicit research setting leaves the section out and logs it. A visible gap is safer than an invented fact every later reader would trust. docs/05 RC-029, HAZ-015
A pixel-spacing mix-up that only real data could reveal
The source files store pixel spacing in a different axis order from this project, and every synthetic test used the project's own order. For one brand, a swap would make a correct outline's fluid volume wrong by a factor of 6.0. A simple size check catches 0 of 210 swapped cases; checking against each brand's known spacing catches all 210. docs/07 §13.3
A data-use question settled by asking
My own reading of the dataset agreement said publishing results might not be allowed. Rather than pick the convenient reading, I asked a challenge organiser, who confirmed that publishing results is permitted. docs/06 §2.2
Reproducibility found to be false, then made true and proven
A resume check passed while a resumed run was seeing data in a different order (D2). One GPU operation fell back to a non-repeatable method 1308 times, with a warning that was easy to miss (D3). Evaluation then turned out not to repeat either: two runs of one model differed in 49 figures. All three are fixed and checked. docs/08
A sealed, pre-registered evaluation
When one assumption written into the plan turned out to be false, I did not run the analysis that depended on it. I decided the replacement, committed it before computing anything, and labelled it post-hoc. docs/07 §19.5

Limitations and threats to validity

  • The familiar-brand test sets are small. 7 patients per run, so only large differences are detectable. This is the main limitation (docs/10 §8.3).
  • The measured gap is a lower bound. Each scan's brightness is normalised on its own, which removes the most obvious brand signature on purpose, so the gap on raw data could be larger (docs/10 §8.1).
  • The score is fragile when a fluid type is absent, as shown under Findings (docs/10 §7.2).
  • Case mix is confounded with brand in the all-scans comparison for SRF and PED (docs/10 §5.2).
  • The expert outlines are taken as truth; their own variability is not quantified here (docs/10 §8.4).
  • Image quality is not separated from appearance shift between brands (docs/10 §8.8).
  • The planned pooling assumption was false, so the pooled rule was decided after the per-run results (docs/10 §8.6).
  • Reproducibility is proven on one machine and its software versions (docs/10 §8.7).

Not done

  • The PACS round trip: written, never run, because Docker is not installed here.
  • Writing the model's results as DICOM files: the builders exist and are tested, but no pipeline step calls them yet.
  • The inference service and the report module are stubs. The model card (docs/12) is still a template.
  • Optional analyses not run: a RETOUCH leaderboard submission, the ablation of brightness normalisation (docs/10 §8.1), and AUROC intervals, which the sealed records cannot provide (docs/08 D9).

About, data and downloads

How this was built

I designed this project and made its decisions: the research question and cross-vendor design, the choice of dataset and how its data agreement was handled, the safety classification, the evaluation protocol written before any results existed, and the calls on what to report and how. I used Claude Code (Anthropic) as a coding assistant.

This page is generated by scripts/08_build_site.py from the evaluation records. No number on it is typed by hand, and tests check that each one matches its source.

Data, credits and licence

This project uses the training data of the RETOUCH challenge, the Retinal OCT Fluid Detection and Segmentation Benchmark and Challenge. I am grateful to the organisers for making the data available to researchers.

Bogunović H, Venhuizen F, Klimscha S, et al. RETOUCH: The Retinal OCT Fluid Detection and Segmentation Benchmark and Challenge. IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging. 2019;38(8):1858-1874. doi:10.1109/TMI.2019.2901398

The data is not redistributed here, in any form: this page shows only per-scan scores and measured summaries, with no images, outlines or identifiers. The data is available from the organisers after registration and carries its own terms of use. The code is MIT-licensed; that licence does not extend to the data.

Downloads

Every table on this page, as CSV. Each file is generated from the evaluation records by the same script as the page.

  • results_per_run.csv: Results per run, fluid type and arm: Dice, HD95, sensitivity, specificity with 95% intervals and n, and AUROC with its positives and negatives
  • results_pooled.csv: Dice pooled across the three runs, patient as the unit (post-hoc)
  • differences.csv: Unseen minus familiar Dice, bootstrapped directly, all scans and fluid-present scans only (post-hoc)
  • per_scan.csv: Every scan's Dice, HD95 and predicted voxel count, per fluid type; no identifiers and no reference presence, sorted by value
  • training.csv: Training loss and validation Dice per epoch, per run
  • dataset.csv: Scan geometry, pixel spacing and fluid prevalence per brand
  • flow.csv: Patients per split bucket and brand, per run
  • The same data as JSON: results.json, per_scan.json, training.json, dataset.json, flow.json, facts.json
